paper_title: Polyphemus: A Palaeolithic Tale? (d'Huy 2014, RMN Newsletter 9, pp. 43-64)
companion_paper: d'Huy 2013a, 'Polyphemus (Aa. Th. 1137): A phylogenetic reconstruction of a prehistoric tale', Nouvelle Mythologie Comparée 1: 3-18 (44 versions x 98 mythemes; used for variant labels and the 2013a Urmärchen text)
extraction_method: Variant list verbatim from Table 2 (d'Huy 2014:49). Character system verbatim from the motif list (Thompson 1961 / Uther 2004, quoted d'Huy 2014:49), the type definition (2014:49), the proto-tale reconstructions (2014:57; 2013a Urmärchen) and the discussion (2014:51-54, n.3). The raw 190-trait binary matrix is NOT printed in the paper (supplementary-only); cells are reconstructed with per-cell provenance (see evidence codes).

evidence_codes.paper_text: d'Huy 2014 / 2013a explicitly states this variant (or the variant's group) carries the character.
evidence_codes.paper_tree_inferred: Inferred from d'Huy's published tree/cluster/reconstruction statements (topology, clade membership, ancestral-state reconstruction).
evidence_codes.canonical_source: Attested content of the variant in the primary sources d'Huy cites (Hackman 1904; Glenn 1978; the cited collections). This is how d'Huy built his own matrix.
evidence_codes.family_standard: Regular within the regional/language-family group per d'Huy's own grouping narrative (European shepherd-form vs Amerindian master-of-animals form).
evidence_codes.unknown: No basis found in the accessible record — state left as '?' (d'Huy's own uncertainty symbol).

characters.name: Giant ogre (Polyphemus)
characters.definition: G100: Giant ogre, Polyphemus (Thompson 1961, list quoted d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Giant
characters.definition: F531: Giant (Uther 2004, list quoted d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Person unusual as to his eyes
characters.definition: F512: Person unusual as to his eyes (Uther 2004, cited d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Deception through false doctoring
characters.definition: K1010: Deception through false doctoring (Uther 2004, cited d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Eye-remedy: blinding under pretext (glowing mass)
characters.definition: K1011: Eye-remedy. Under the pretence of curing his eyesight, the trickster blinds the dupe (Often with a glowing mass thrust into the eye) (Thompson 1961, quoted d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Escape by disguise
characters.definition: K521: Escape by disguise (Uther 2004, cited d'Huy 2014:49). d'Huy codes only the escape-from-the-cave motif (K521; K603).

characters.name: Escape by dressing in animal (bird, human) skin
characters.definition: K521.1: Escape by dressing in animal (bird, human) skin (Thompson 1961, quoted d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: 'Noman' name trick
characters.definition: K602: "Noman" (Thompson 1961, quoted d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Escape under ram's belly
characters.definition: K603: Escape under ram's belly (Thompson 1961, quoted d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Magic objects betray fugitive
characters.definition: D1612.1: Magic objects betray fugitive. Give alarm when fugitive escapes (Uther 2004, quoted d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Master/lord of (wild) animals as host
characters.definition: Type definition: the hero 'gets into the homestead of a master of animals or of a monstrous shepherd' (d'Huy 2014:49). 'a lord of wild animals similar to Amerindian versions found in the Valais corpus' (2014:51-52); 'a master of the beasts similar to Amerindian versions' (2013a:9).

characters.name: Monstrous shepherd as host (domestic flocks)
characters.definition: Type definition: host is 'a monstrous shepherd' (d'Huy 2014:49); 'The supernatural shepherd of European traditions is equivalent to the lord of animals in his control of resources' (2014:51-52).

characters.name: Host wants to kill the hero
characters.definition: Type definition: 'the host wants to kill the hero, but the hero escapes...' (d'Huy 2014:49); 'A monster tries to kill the hero' (2013a Urmärchen).

characters.name: Escape by clinging to fleece/fur of outgoing animal
characters.definition: Type definition: 'the hero escapes by holding on to the fleece or fur of an animal who is going out' (d'Huy 2014:49); '[To escape, the hero clings to a living animal.]' (proto, 2014:57).

characters.name: Escape by concealing under an animal's skin
characters.definition: Type definition: 'concealing himself under an animal's skin' (d'Huy 2014:49).

characters.name: Escape with a living animal
characters.definition: Type definition: 'or with a living animal' (d'Huy 2014:49); '[To escape, the hero clings to a living animal.]' (2014:57).

characters.name: Hero enters the monster's house/hut
characters.definition: 'A human hunter enters in the monster's house' (proto, 2014:57); 'He enters the monster's house' (Neolithic reconstruction, 2014:57); 'He enters in the homestead of the monster uninvited' (2013a).

characters.name: Monster traps hero + animals with immovable/large door
characters.definition: '[He traps the man and his own animals with an immovable or a large door.]' (2014:57; brackets = 50-75% reconstruction confidence); 'the entrance is blocked with a great stone or a locked door. Animals are locked' (2013a).

characters.name: Monster waits at the entrance to kill hero / checks animals
characters.definition: 'The monster waits for the man near the entrance to kill him' (Neolithic reconstruction, 2014:57); 'checks the animals that go away' (2013a); 'the monster who controls the beasts from his dwelling' (2014:54).

characters.name: Vengeance connected with fire (blinding element)
characters.definition: 'a vengeance occurs that is connected with fire' (2014:57); the fire/glowing-mass side of K1011. Reconstructed at the root with >75% confidence; features 'correlate with the Amerindian traditions' (2014:57).

characters.name: Giant with one eye in the forehead
characters.definition: 'a giant who has one eye in the forehead' (Neolithic reconstruction, 2014:57).

characters.name: Enemy is a completely solitary figure
characters.definition: 'The enemy is a completely solitary figure, a giant...' (2014:57). Contrast 2013a Urmärchen: 'There are at least two monsters' (2013a:16) — a reconstruction conflict noted in the 2014 paper's own re-analysis.

characters.name: Monster possesses a herd of WILD animals
characters.definition: 'The monster possesses herd of wild animals' (Palaeolithic reconstruction, 2014:57); 'they live in a tent and possess a herd of wild animals' (2013a).

characters.name: Monster possesses a herd of domestic animals (sheep)
characters.definition: 'The monster possesses a herd of domestic animals (sheep)' (Neolithic reconstruction, 2014:57); the sheep-holding form is tied to sheep domestication 9-11 kya in Mesopotamia (2014:57).

characters.name: Hero perceives a light in the distance; does not know whom he will meet
characters.definition: 'A human [perceives a light in the distance and does not know whom he will meet]' (2014:57; brackets = 50-75%).

characters.name: Hero hides INSIDE an animal (entering through its anus)
characters.definition: '...the hero often hides inside an animal itself by entering through its anus. This enables the hero to escape the monster who controls the beasts from his dwelling' (d'Huy 2014:54, Amerindian versions; also his Trois-Freres rock-art reading).

characters.name: Valais: dwarf punishes hero by creating an avalanche
characters.definition: 'the dwarf (structural inversion of the giant) tries to punish the hero by creating an avalanche' (d'Huy 2014, note 3); linked to archaic Tyrolian giant-lore protecting sheep and punishing with avalanches.

characters.name: Curse pronounced by the blinded giant on the hero
characters.definition: Homeric form (Odyssey IX): Polyphemus' curse on Odysseus invoking Poseidon; character not in d'Huy's motif list but part of the Homeric variant he includes ('such the Homeric one' cluster discussion, 2014:59).

characters.name: Seafaring/voyage frame (cyclops met during a voyage)
characters.definition: Homeric form (Odyssey IX): the adventure occurs during Odysseus' voyage; absent from landlocked variants.

characters.name: Hero is a hunter
characters.definition: 'The hero is a hunter' (2013a Urmärchen); 'A human hunter enters in the monster's house' (2014:57). European variants mostly replace the hunter with a shepherd/wanderer.

The archaic European outlier: 'the Valais is probably the most archaic European version; it is intermediate between European and Amerindian corpus, with a master of the beasts similar to Amerindian versions' (2013a:9); 'a lord of wild animals similar to Amerindian versions found in the Valais corpus' (2014:51); ends with 'the dwarf (structural inversion of the giant) [who] tries to punish the hero by creating an avalanche' (2014 n.3); 'intermediate situation of the Valais' and Ojibwa versions (2014:53). Root of both trees runs between Ojibwa and Valais (2014:51).

2013a: 'Mediterranean people (first cluster: Greek 1, Berber 3, Serbian)'.

Ralston's 'One-Eyed Likho' (first-cited source): a blacksmith blinds the one-eyed forest-demon with a red-hot iron; no flock, no ram escape; the blinded Likho clings to the man's back in pursuit and is killed at the river. Coded per this source-critical reading; NOTE the tension with d'Huy's tree, which places 'Israeli, Berber and Russian' versions in a Homeric-adjacent clade (2014:59) - his 190-trait coding evidently captured features (or the Karel/Erben complement) that our 30-character projection cannot see.
Richter's 'Der einaugige Riese' ('the one-eyed giant').
Baring-Gould's 'The Giant of New Mills, Sessay'; 2014:58 — early European diffusion wave includes Basque, Oghuz Turks, Yorkshire and the West Highlands (Celtic/Brittonic + Galatian hypothesis).
Goidelic variant; same early-diffusion cluster as Yorkshire/Basque/Oghuz (2014:58).

caveats: Table 2 family counts sum to 54 while the abstract reports 56 variants; 2 units cannot be enumerated from the paper (likely within Italic=10, of which 8 entries are named, and/or Afro-Asiatic=6). Units reaching each family count are marked 'reconstructed' in notes.

The 30-character projection is NOT d'Huy's raw 190-trait coding. It is the intersection of (a) his printed motif list, (b) his type definition, (c) his two ancestral-state reconstructions, and (d) canonical variant content from the cited primary sources. Tree statistics (RI etc.) from the paper are not directly comparable.

Characters have uneven coverage: regional signatures (master-of-animals, hide-inside-animal, sheep-herd, fire-blinding) are well supported; fine-grained details (Noman, light-in-distance, solitary) are '?' for most variants and act as near-singletons.
d'Huy's own matrix used '?' for uncertainty; we do the same.
